item.title: Supreme Court sides with GOP in fight over discounted ads ahead of midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By John Kruzel WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court again sided with Republicans on Wednesday in the latest clash over a new Federal Communications Commission policy that gives party committees access to discounted TV and radio advertising rates long available to political candidates. The court agreed to ‌let the FCC, which is chaired by Trump ally Brendan Carr, avoid a judicially imposed deadline that would have forced the agency to rule ‌on a Democratic challenge to the policy before the November 3 midterm elections. The FCC joined two Republican committees in filing a request to the Supreme Court to lift the lower court's deadline. The court ​has a 6-3 conservative majority. Liberal Justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson indicated they would have denied the request. The FCC, which currently has a 2-1 Republican majority, modified its so-called "lowest unit charge" rule in March in a move seen as a boost to President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans. The president's party is seeking to retain control of Congress in the November 3 midterms. "We are pleased the Supreme Court has granted the FCC's stay request. The court's decision is right on the law and avoids the specter of upending ‌the rules for political ads right in the middle of ⁠an ongoing election," an FCC spokesperson said. Chief Justice John Roberts had previously lifted the October 9 deadline that was given to the FCC by the Richmond-based 4th US Circuit Court of Appeals. The 4th Circuit has accused the FCC of repeated "delay tactics" in ⁠the case, and emphasized the need for an urgent ruling in the Democratic challenge given the looming election. The Supreme Court's latest action marks the second time in recent weeks that it has addressed the FCC's policy, as major Republican committees head toward the midterms with a cash advantage over their Democratic counterparts. In September, the court granted a request by the national Republican ​committees ​that support the party's candidates in Senate and House of Representatives races to revive the policy ​after the 4th Circuit blocked it. The justices in an ‌8-1 ruling said that the Democratic candidates must wait for the FCC to rule before filing a challenge in court. The FCC policy at issue requires broadcasters to charge discounted rates for airing certain political advertisements within 60 days of a general election, a window that opened this year on September 4. A group of Democratic candidates including Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia in April challenged the policy through in-house proceedings at the FCC. When the agency took no action, the Democrats successfully challenged the policy in the 4th Circuit, a ruling that was later halted by the Supreme Court. The 4th Circuit on October 7 ordered the FCC to issue a prompt ruling on the ‌Democratic in-house challenge, more than five months after it was filed. In its 2-1 ruling, the ​4th Circuit said its "willingness to tolerate the FCC's delay tactics is at an end." 'TRENCH WARFARE' The Republican committees ​in their Supreme Court filing accused the 4th Circuit of having "short-circuited" the ​FCC's review process. The Democratic candidates, for their part, accused the FCC in court papers of engaging in "blatant procedural trench warfare to stave ‌off judicial review of an unlawful agency directive until it is ​too late to matter." The FCC policy gained ​greater significance after the Supreme Court in June struck down federal restrictions on spending coordinated between parties and their candidates, siding with Republican challengers including Vice President JD Vance. Since the June ruling, Republican committees have blown past the former limits ahead of the midterms. The two Republican committees have exceeded the ​former national caps by more than $48 million, according to Federal ‌Election Commission spending disclosures for July and August. Their Democratic counterparts also eclipsed the former limits, but by much less — just under $4 million. The three ​main national Republican committees ended August with about $233 million in cash. Their Democratic counterparts held roughly $130 million but also carried nearly $18 million in ​debt, according to Federal Election Commission filings. (Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/us-supreme-court-again-backs-204225313.html

item.title: Can Trump strip Ilhan Omar of her U.S. citizenship? It's not that simple.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference at the US Capitol on Feb. 24, 2026, in Washington, D.C. —Daniel Heuer—Bloomberg via Getty Images In a highly unusual step, federal agents this week aggressively intensified their investigations into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, weeks before she stands for reelection in her home district. The Department of Justice on Tuesday subpoenaed relatives of Omar’s family members, including her sister Sahra Noor, according to The New York Times . The grand jury subpoenas were issued shortly after a raid of the lawmaker’s residence in Washington, D.C. on Monday. The judicial search warrant, which is under seal, was executed by Homeland Security Investigations, the investigative branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement . Although the Department of Justice did not provide any more details of the investigation, multiple outlets , citing anonymous sources, reported that the search stemmed from Omar’s immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child. Prior to the investigation, multiple Trump Administration officials have accused Omar of immigration fraud without presenting any evidence. In a podcast interview in March, Vice President JD Vance said the White House was exploring “legal remedies” to her alleged immigration fraud. Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the investigation into Omar was “ongoing” and dismissed efforts to frame the case as political retribution. “If we actually move a case forward, it’s not a political case. It's actually a case because they did things wrong,” Mullin said during the interview with right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson. Omar, who has long denied the allegations, condemned the raid on her home as “political intimidation” and said she will “not be silenced.” President Trump, along with many MAGA Republicans, has repeatedly floated the idea of revoking Omar’s citizenship, a process also known as denaturalization, and deporting her. But legal and immigration experts tell TIME that denaturalizing a U.S. citizen is a rare and difficult process, one that requires federal authorities to clear a high bar in front of a federal judge. Here’s what to know about how the process works. How does denaturalization work? Stripping someone of their citizenship is a more arduous legal process than most other immigration efforts that involve the courts. Deportation proceedings, for instance, are initiated by ICE agents under the Department of Homeland Security and are then approved by immigration judges who are hired and work within the Department of Justice. The denaturalization process, on the other hand, must be approved by an independent federal judge, who evaluates the request by a higher standard. All denaturalization efforts begin at DOJ. In order to revoke a naturalized person’s citizenship, a DOJ lawyer must decide whether to file a civil or a criminal petition in court. Yuripzy Morgan, an attorney and host of Free Range National podcase, said a civil complaint does not have a statute of limitation, whereas a criminal complaint has a statute of limitation of 10 years and must clear a much higher legal bar. “For civil denaturalization, the government has to show that there is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence that the person in question obtained their naturalization either illegally, or they willfully misrepresented a material fact, ” Morgan says. She stressed that simply having an error in an immigration document doesn't mean that a judge is going to approve stripping a person of their citizenship. For a criminal denaturalization conviction, the federal government must show “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” that the individual knowingly obtained citizenship through fraud, which is the highest legal standard of proof required to secure a criminal conviction. In 2017, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Maslenjak v. United States that only an illegal act that played a role in a person’s citizenship application could lead to criminal denaturalization, further narrowing down the scope of such efforts. Omar’s father filled out and submitted her citizenship application on her behalf when she was 17. It is unclear what evidence, if any, the federal government has to show that anything in the application was fraudulent, or that Omar or her father intentionally misrepresented anything in that application. Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and a resident fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies, pointed out that even after someone gets denaturalized, a deportation is not guaranteed. The person would still be able to retain their previous legal immigration status until a final order of removal is issued to the person by ICE. “If they had a green card before they naturalized, even after they get denaturalized, they are going to have a green card,” Arthur says. How did Rep. Omar get naturalized as a U.S. citizen? According to Omar’s House biography, Omar and her family fled her home country Somalia when she was eight. The family eventually sought asylum in the United States in 1995. She told The New York Times that she became a U.S. citizen in 2000 when she was 17. At the time Omar went through the process, federal law allowed immigrants under the age of 18 to get naturalized as U.S. citizens if both of their parents had become U.S. citizens. The law was eventually replaced by a new law in 2001, which only requires one parent to become a citizen for the children to be naturalized. At the center of this investigation is whether Omar’s father, Nur Omar Mohamed, lied about her age in immigration documents so she could be eligible to derive citizenship through him, according to The Washington Post , which cited two unnamed sources. According to Arthur, the former immigration judge, if Omar was 18 at the time of the naturalization application, she may have been able to apply for her citizenship on her own after having a valid green card for five years. The allegations regarding Omar’s citizenship gained attention among conservative activists and commentators starting in 2019, when Omar became a member of Congress. Shortly after her election, Omar’s staff sought to change her official birth year in public records from 1981 to 1982, according to multiple outlets . How often does the U.S. government strip people of their citizenship? Despite the renewed push from the second Trump administration, denaturalization remains an exceedingly rare legal process. According to the Migration Policy Institute , a Washington, D.C.-based think tank, an average of 11 denaturalization cases were filed per year between 1990 and 2017. Denaturalization efforts have increased in Trump’s second term. The DOJ has announced efforts to strip at least 108 people of their citizenship in 2026. That is still considerably smaller than the hundreds of thousands of people whom the U.S. government grants citizenship to through naturalization every year. This article originally appeared on Time at https://time.com/article/2026/10/14/ilhan-omar-citizenship-investigation-denaturalization-DOJ/

item.title: U.S. may have withheld warnings to Ukraine on deadly Kyiv strikes
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The U.S. may have intentionally withheld early warnings this week of Russian strikes on Ukraine , multiple sources familiar with the matter told CBS News. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine "received no advance warning from our partners" when Russia launched a ballistic missile barrage at Kyiv and other locations early Tuesday. The sources said American officials told their Ukrainian counterparts the system used to detect Russian missile launches had failed due to "bad weather." Ukrainian officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the topic, told CBS News they did not believe the excuse, and they accused the U.S. instead of "playing" with the system. When Russia launched another wave of ballistic missiles around 3 a.m. local time on Wednesday, the sources said the U.S. early warning system appeared to be working again. The sources said the U.S. had failed to provide intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches during one previous instance earlier this year, citing the need to focus more resources on the Middle East. Zelenskyy said Wednesday that Russia launched more than 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions during the overnight attack, primarily targeting energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv and Kharkiv, killing six people and leaving some 600,000 without power. President Trump, asked Tuesday if the U.S. had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, said: "No, we haven't. We help them, but we're really helping them get to a final answer. We want the war ended." "We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end, so we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end," Mr. Trump said. Russia started launching strikes soon after Mr. Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire." Earlier this week, the Trump administration threatened to stop sharing intelligence and to halt the purchase of U.S.-made weapons by European allies for Ukraine via the PURL procurement system if Ukraine did not stop deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure, a European and a Ukrainian official told CBS News. Ukraine relies on U.S. intelligence for both offensive and defensive military capabilities, including data from satellites and aircraft sensors used to identify launches of Russian aircraft and missiles. Sources familiar with the matter told CBS News the U.S. had not ceased intelligence sharing with Ukraine overall — calling the lack of a warning about this week's attacks a specific incident. Ukrainian officials and soldiers also told CBS News that Ukraine's military had started experiencing difficulties Tuesday night and Wednesday morning with Starlink, the satellite technology owned by SpaceX's Elon Musk. In an interview with CBS News earlier this year, Ukraine's former minister of defense Mykhailo Fedorov said Starlink was one of Ukraine's most important technologies, as it allows Ukrainian soldiers to communicate and carry out strikes in environments saturated by electronic warfare. "On the night of 14 October, without warning the Defence Forces, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals ('military package') while in motion. This complicates UAV missions, particularly interceptors and middle-strike drones, and reduces capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance and signal relay," sources in Ukraine's Ministry of Defense told CBS News. "At present, the Ministry of Defence is in contact with the United States, SpaceX and NATO partners, is collecting data from all units, and backup communication channels are being tested and put into use." The Starlink restrictions were first reported by the Kyiv Independent and the Financial Times. CBS News has reached out to SpaceX, the White House, and the Pentagon for comment. On Wednesday, as President Zelenskyy arrived in the United Kingdom to meet with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other officials, he called for a U.S. response to the recent Russian strikes. "The strike was absolutely deliberate and indicative in its scale — such a demonstrative disrespect from Russia toward America has never happened before. Russia does not consider the statements of the President of America to be strong," he wrote on X. "We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to respond, and to respond harshly." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/us-ukraine-intelligence-russia-war-missile-strikes-kyiv-power-outages/

item.title: Social Security benefits are getting their biggest boost since 2023. But there's a catch.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Social Security and SSI benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027 for more than 72 million people, the Social Security Administration (SSA) announced today. The cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is the biggest since 2023 and means, on average, retirement benefits will rise by $75 a month, SSA said. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) says that works out to roughly $900 a year, and estimates the highest earners will see an increase of more than $2,200 a year. SSA calculates the COLA based on the average year-over-year change in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (a form of measuring inflation) for July, August and September. SSI recipients will see the first higher payment on Dec. 31, 2026. Some people receive both SSI and Social Security. Most Social Security recipients will be paid the higher amount starting Jan. 1, 2027. The COLA will also affect Medicare Part B beneficiaries, whose premiums are deducted from their Social Security payments. The 2027 standard premium is projected to rise to $209.50 from $202.90, an increase of $6.60 a month, which would leave the average retired worker about $68 a month better off after COLA. 'Next year's COLA can't come soon enough' SSA Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said the adjustment will give beneficiaries "greater financial stability," and reflects a year of elevated inflation, particularly in gasoline and energy prices. But Nancy Altman, president of the advocacy group Social Security Works, said the increase "doesn't fully account for the costs that Social Security beneficiaries face." Altman said that's because the CPI-W, the inflation index used to calculate Social Security increases, tracks the costs of working people, not retirees, who she said spend a higher share of their income on health care and housing. "Next year's COLA can't come soon enough for many Social Security beneficiaries," she told Yahoo. The Senior Citizens League (TSCL), a nonpartisan seniors' group, was also critical of the payment increase. Executive director Shannon Benton said in a statement that the COLA "falls short of expectations" and that benefits lag behind price spikes because seniors don't see the adjustment until January. It's a concern also shared by beneficiaries. AARP analysis released this week found that 76% of adults 50 and older said a COLA of around 3.5%, slightly lower than the announced figure, would not be enough to help them keep up with rising prices. Kathleen Romig, director of Social Security and disability policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said the annual COLA increase is "especially important in times of high inflation." "This year's COLA is bigger than in many recent years because of rising prices," she told Yahoo. "Another 3.6% … will help beneficiaries keep up with rising costs at the pump and in the grocery store." Some policy groups say the COLA calculation should be updated to use a measure that better reflects retirees' spending habits. The Senior Citizens League wants COLA for retirees to be calculated based on a metric called the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E) . Introduced by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in 1987, it uses the same underlying price collection system as the main CPI, but instead calculates the market basket to reflect how older Americans actually spend their money , taking a snapshot of retirees' spending priorities as well as how much they spend out of pocket. How do I check if I'm eligible for the increase? You don't need to do anything. The increase is automatic for everyone receiving Social Security or SSI. SSA said enrollees can see their 2027 Medicare Part B premium in their "my Social Security Message Center" starting in late November. Medicare changes will be posted at medicare.gov. Beneficiaries will receive a simplified, one-page COLA notice with their new benefit amount, exact dates and any deductions. Online: People with a personal my Social Security account can view the notice starting in late November, up to three weeks before a mailed notice. People without an account need to create one and enroll in paperless notices by Nov. 18 to see it online. Account holders can also sign up for text or email alerts. By mail: Anyone not enrolled in paperless notices will get theirs in December. For more information, see SSA's COLA page . Key dates Nov. 18: Deadline to create a my Social Security account and enroll in paperless notices to see the notice online. Late November: Online COLA notices will become available to paperless account holders, and Medicare enrollees can see their 2027 Part B premium in their Message Center. The premium is typically deducted directly from monthly Social Security payments. December: Mailed COLA notices go out. Dec. 31, 2026 to January 2027: Beneficiaries begin receiving payments with the increase added. SSI payments normally arrive on the first of the month, but the January payment will arrive on Dec. 31, 2026, because Jan. 1 is a federal holiday. Social Security payments generally go out on the second, third or fourth Wednesday of the month, based on the beneficiary's birthday. People who began receiving Social Security before May 1997, or who receive both Social Security and SSI, generally get their Social Security payment on the third of the month. This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/article/social-securitys-cola-is-the-biggest-since-2023-americans-will-get-an-extra-75-a-month-on-average-142530711.html

item.title: Reflecting Pool liner failed in 85 places, inspection finds
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A recently applied blue coating on the bottom of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was damaged in at least 85 places after workers rushed to refill the pool before the Donald Trump-requested liner had set. A report commissioned by the contractor that did the work, obtained by The Washington Post , does not make any mention of vandalism despite the president’s ongoing claims and sworn statements from administration officials that attributed the peeled-off lining to “botched installation.” The report instead blames a rushed job to meet Trump’s demands that the work be completed for the nation’s 250th anniversary on July 4. The 75-page “failure analysis” by Atlantic Coating Inspection reveals that Trump’s “American flag blue” coating buckled along eight of the 10 expansion joints on the pool’s basin. The liner also blistered in nearly 40 places due to moisture or chemical fumes trapped beneath it, and the paint peeled in nearly two dozen spots before detaching from the pool floor and flapping to the surface, the report found. A ‘failure analysis’ found more than 85 damage points at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool that compromised a recently applied blue liner after Donald Trump pushed for renovations this summer (Reuters) The Trump administration has funneled nearly $20 million in taxpayer funding into the project despite the president’s initial estimate that the renovation could be done quickly for just $1.5 million. That was in April. The liner was finally replaced in recent weeks and the pool is being refilled, again, this week. Initial costs quickly surged to nearly $7 million this summer after an initial no-bid contract was handed to a Virginia-based firm that did not appear to have previously held a contract with the federal government. That company, Atlantic Industrial Coatings LLC, was awarded another $6.2 million in May, according to federal spending records. On June 3, the company received another $1 million — followed by more than $461,000 on June 15. The shallow pool, which the president repeatedly promotes as “bigger than skyscrapers,” was initially refurbished this summer with a shade of dark blue and outfitted with “advanced nanobubbler technology” to tackle algae blooms that have long plagued the landmark. But shortly after workers refilled the pool, the algae returned, and the recently applied sealant in the Trump-requested blue hue started to peel and float to the surface. The monument was then closed off with fencing and the pool was drained once again to repair the damage and redo the work. In July, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said the Trump administration would not seek any new contracts after costs for the project exploded to more than $17 million. But spending records show that the National Park Service awarded a nearly $2.7 million contract to American Ag Energy Inc. the following month for the maintenance, repair and rebuilding of water purification and sewage treatment equipment. Another firm, Ohio-based Green Water Solutions, also known as Greenwater Services, was also awarded $1.8 million to install a water-purification system. Workers have been forced to drain the pool and re-do renovations after administration officials admitted that damage to the monument was due to ‘botched’ construction, not vandalism, despite the president’s claims (AP) The Department of Interior skipped a typical competitive bidding process to hand out millions of taxpayer dollars to a handful of companies for the work, claiming that “only a limited pool of contractors possess the qualification and equipment” for the work, Officials claimed that the need for renovations was so urgent that any delays would cause “serious injury” to the government, though it remains unclear what that “injury” entailed. In July, weeks after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro publicly accused a former Olympian of “forcefully and violently” ripping out the blue liner, she dismissed a criminal case against him entirely. Pirro’s office admitted that the Trump-requested “American flag blue” sealant started to peel “almost immediately” after the work was completed after recent renovations to the site. The Department of Interior “provided less than fulsome information at the outset of this case,” the filing said. It was not until after the indictment was filed against 67-year-old David Hearn that the agency determined that the “damage was the result of a botched installation and not vandalism,” according to Pirro’s office. Trump later pushed Pirro to “revisit her hastily made decision,” though he has also admitted that “some contractor error” played a role in the damage. A judge in Washington, DC, has blocked prosecutors from trying to charge David Hearn a second time after the government dismissed a criminal case against him over damage to the monument (Getty) A judge later blocked prosecutors from trying to charge Hearn a second time , finding that a case against him would likely be the result of “political pressure” from the president. Earlier this month, D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman called that idea of prosecuting Hearn again “simply fanciful” and permanently tossed the case against him. Hearn’s attorneys have asked the Department of Justice and Department of Interior to launch an independent investigation into alleged “widespread misconduct” surrounding the case. The administration “subjected an innocent man to a nightmare of wrongful arrest, felony indictment, and public defamation to cover up their own botched, rushed renovation of the Reflecting Pool,” attorneys Michael Bromwich, Steve Levin, Norm Eisen and Mary Dohrmann said in a statement last week, “This administration threw the entire weight of the federal government into prosecuting Davey Hearn, and their actions surrounding his arrest and indictment demand full accountability,” they added. This article originally appeared on The Independent at https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/trump-reflecting-pool-inspection-damage-report-b3066749.html

item.title: FBI investigates suspicious powder sent to election officials in 3 states
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Oct. 14 (UPI) -- Election officials in Ohio, Louisiana and Oklahoma said they were sent packages containing suspicious white powder, prompting law enforcement to investigate. The suspicious powder was discovered in Louisiana and Oklahoma on Tuesday, while a similar mailing intended for Ohio was intercepted Wednesday. Louisiana Secretary of State Nancy Landry said in a statement that her office in Baton Rouge was closed Tuesday after an Elections Division employee opened a package at around 12:20 p.m. CDT and found white powder inside. The Oklahoma State Election Board said in a statement it received an envelope containing a "suspicious white powder" on Tuesday morning. And a statement from Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose on Wednesday states that U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a letter containing "a powdery white substance" intended for his office. The offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma were evacuated, while the Louisiana office was closed for the remainder of Tuesday. LaRose said investigators who intercepted the envelope intended for his Ohio office were "dealing with similar mailings sent to election officials in multiple states." He said the FBI was handling the matter. "We have informed our county boards of elections to be vigilant in the days ahead," he said. Landry stated Tuesday that her office did not know what the substance was, but law enforcement was responding to the incident. The Oklahoma State Election Board said the Oklahoma Highway Patrol was "immediately" notified after it received the envelope. "Thankfully, no one from the State Election Board staff was harmed as a result of this incident," State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax said. "We want to assure Oklahoma voters that today's incident does not impact our ability to conduct elections. Election officials remain committed to ensuring safe and secure elections." The FBI told NBC News in a statement that it was working with its partners to identify those behind the letters, while declining to confirm where letters had been received. The incidents come just weeks before Nov. 3 midterm elections. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement Wednesday that they are "deeply concerned by these incidents." "As we have each stated in the past, threats against election officials and workers have no place in our democracy. Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties," it said. This article originally appeared on United Press International at https://www.upi.com/Top_News/US/2026/10/14/Ohio-Louisiana-Oklahoma-white-powder/7831792031234/

item.title: Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia faces complaint over claims she's a lawyer
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Newly appointed White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia in Washington, D.C., on October 13, 2026. (Photo by Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images) A government watchdog group filed a complaint Wednesday with the State Bar of California, seeking an investigation into newly appointed White House press secretary Katie Zacharia over allegations she falsely represented herself as a lawyer despite apparently never having been licensed to practice. Campaign for Accountability alleges that Zacharia might have violated California law by repeatedly identifying herself as a lawyer on television and serving as general counsel for a California nonprofit organization. "If that reporting is accurate, Ms. Zacharia has repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so, conduct California law treats as a crime," the complaint stated. Rick Coca, a spokesperson for the State Bar of California, confirmed the agency had no record of Zacharia being licensed in California under her married or maiden names. "Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie," CfA Executive Director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a news release. "In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime," she said. White House Communications Director Steven Cheung responded on X , calling CfA a "radical-leftist organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome." "Nobody takes them seriously because they are deranged low lifes," Cheung wrote. InfluenceWatch, a project of the conservative Capital Research Center, describes CfA as a left-of-center advocacy group that frequently targets Republican officials and conservative organizations. It notes the group was founded by former staff members of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Government and has two prominent Democrat political operatives on its board. The complaint cites several instances in which Zacharia described herself as a lawyer, including an Oct. 5 appearance on Newsmax anchor Greg Kelly’s WABC radio show, when she invoked her legal background while discussing the Senate’s use of blue slips in the confirmation process for U.S. attorneys. It also questions her reported tenure as general counsel for Fix California, a nonprofit founded by former Trump administration official Richard Grenell, from January 2024 to March 2025. CfA acknowledged it is unknown whether Zacharia performed legal work for Fix California and asked the State Bar to investigate her responsibilities. Under California law, unauthorized practice of law or unlawfully representing oneself as entitled to practice law can constitute a misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in county jail, a $1,000 fine, or both. The complaint asks regulators to consider referring the matter to prosecutors if violations are established. Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine University School of Law in 2011, previously worked for the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing. Asked Wednesday where she passed the bar exam, Zacharia responded , "when I moved to China." A White House official told The Hill she worked on international transaction law in China after relocating there with her husband. President Donald Trump described Zacharia as "an attorney" when announcing her appointment last week. Material from The Associated Press was used in this report. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved.This article originally appeared on Newsmax at https://www.newsmax.com/newsfront/katie-zacharia-white-house-california-bar/2026/10/14/id/1272822

item.title: Ukraine relies on Starlink to fight Russia. Now a sudden change threatens its drones.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
[Getty Images] Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on. Kyiv has adopted it as a vital battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare. Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones are able to maintain stronger connections with operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming. But a sudden speed restriction for drones connected to Starlink means some battlefield "missions" have been disrupted, according to a top Ukrainian official. Serhiy Beskrestnov also said officials had not been told about the 100mph (160km/h) speed limits set overnight on Tuesday by Elon Musk's SpaceX company. Throttling drones connected to the network at this relatively low speed makes Ukrainian efforts to intercept jet-powered Russian drones all but useless, according to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW). Musk's network of satellites makes Ukrainian drone operators more effective [Getty Images] Starlink is "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", the institute's George Barros says, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces. Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft told the BBC that the restrictions could have major implications as the technology allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimized." Starlink does not work inside Russia, but Ukrainian drones can use the satellites to communicate back to their operators during strikes. There is no ready replacement for the network. Starlink-enabled interceptors are also among Ukraine's most effective solution against jet-powered Russian Shahed drones, he said. Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph, meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible. Tom Whittington, electronic warfare expert and associate fellow at RUSI, told BBC Radio 4's PM programme that the satellite system allows Ukraine to move large amounts of data - like video, text and voice calls - in a similar way that smartphones do but without the infrastructure that phones need. The speed restrictions "effectively preclude" anything connected to the network going above 100mph, Whittington said, making drone navigation difficult within Ukraine and Russian-occupied territory inside Ukraine. Serhiy Beskrestnov - Zelensky's adviser - says he believes the restrictions are not a coincidence and are related to the latest strains between Kyiv and Washington. US President Donald Trump has criticised Ukraine's long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and called for a new leader - criticisms which have been echoed by Elon Musk. Ukraine's complaint about the restrictions has drawn attention to both Starlink, and Starshield - a military-grade version of the network developed for the Pentagon by SpaceX. Musk says the two systems are separate, but in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology. And in a post on X , Musk suggested the US government could be responsible for the slowdown afflicting Ukrainian usage of the technology. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," he wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS. "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory. SpaceX's satellite communications have proved vital to both armies during the four-year war, including a Russian attack on a moving passenger train , but earlier this year Musk cut the use of Starlink terminals for Russian forces in a move that blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders . item.title: As inflation rises, poll finds 4 in 10 Americans struggle to afford basic necessities
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
More than 4 in 10 Americans said they are struggling to afford basic living costs amid rising inflation levels in the country, according to polling data released Wednesday. The Pew Research Center surveys , which were conducted in late July and August, found that 44 percent of U.S. adults reported struggling to pay for basic necessities like medical care, rent or mortgage, transportation and food. Rising costs had an even greater impact on lower income Americans, as 71 percent of those surveyed said they struggled with costs for at least one of these expense categories. Additionally, 60 percent of people said they did not have enough income to “lead the kind of life they want,” while 53 percent said they did not have sufficient emergency funds. The inflation rate in August was 3.4 percent , down from 3.7 percent in July. Since then, the Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported further increases to the consumer price index, including a 0.6 percent increase in September. Gas prices have accounted for a sizable share of the inflation rate increases, as the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war placed a sustained strain on global energy supplies. A gallon of regular gas was around $4.33 a gallon in the U.S. on Wednesday afternoon, up from about $3.08 a year ago, according to AAA . The average cost of diesel has also spiked to more than $6 a gallon — an increase of more than $2 from last year. President Trump has attempted to calm concerns about rising costs of living amid this conflict and his administration’s tariff fight with Canada ahead of the midterm elections, in which affordability is expected to be a top issue for voters at the ballot box. During a Tuesday campaign rally in Alaska, the president did not offer hope that the months-long conflict was nearing a close, telling the crowd he has “had it” with Iran’s leaders and added that his administration was “going to do a number” on the country. The Pew report released Wednesday was based on findings from two surveys among a sample of 5,166 U.S. adults with a margin of error of approximately 1.6 percentage points. One poll was conducted from Aug. 24-30, while the other was conducted from July 20 to Aug. 9. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. item.title: A mysterious death in Russia renews fears about ancient viruses trapped in Siberia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The unexplained death this month of a Russian lab technician at a Siberian facility for the study of dangerous pathogens raised global anxieties over the potential for an outbreak of pneumonic plague. But while the cause of concern - bound up in a lack of transparency from Moscow - was new, Russia’s frozen hinterlands have long been the source of a separate fear that they could harbor disease risks for which the world is not prepared. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Russian authorities imposed containment measures after the 28-year-old’s death from what they said was pneumonia of “unknown origins,” prompting the United States to ask for more information. A World Health Organization report released Saturday said that Russian authorities found no signs of an outbreak of plague or some other infectious disease, but did not provide sufficient details to identify the origin of the woman’s illness or say whether exposure at work played a role in it. Siberia’s vast wilderness harbors natural reservoirs of pathogens, from fleas that spread plague found in marmots and squirrels to ticks bearing encephalitis to the ancient pathogens frozen in the layer of permafrost. The Russian institute where the lab technician worked was set up in the 1930s as a plague prevention station to curb outbreaks of the deadly bacterial disease that periodically affected local populations as well as people in neighboring Mongolia and China’s Manchuria region. The disease, for which early antibiotic treatments were pioneered that decade, could be spread through contact with marmots, which were hunted for meat and sometimes eaten undercooked or even raw, like in a 2019 case of a Mongolian couple. The settlement of Siberia, which had a 19th-century gold rush and served as a place of exile for criminals under the Russian Empire, connected the remote region to the western parts of the empire and raised the risk of plague spreading farther west, much as epidemic diseases from European Russia, such as cholera and typhus, easily reached Siberia through migrating workers and because of the near-total absence of medical care. A study published this year suggested that the bands of hunter-gatherers who inhabited the Lake Baikal region were the victims of the earliest known plague outbreak, about 5,500 years ago. To this day, plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian Far East, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents. Human cases in Russia are rare, however. The country’s last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in the Altai region contracted plague after contact with a marmot. The threat of dangerous disease comes not only from wildlife but also from the millennia-old microbes and viruses stored in the permafrost that underlies the vast majority of the region. About a decade ago, a group of researchers isolated “zombie viruses” from Siberian permafrost, raising fears that a new global medical emergency could be triggered by a disease from the distant past. The permafrost, a dark, cold, oxygenless mass, is a perfect storage container for biological material, and scientists believe that at its deepest levels it may contain viruses up to a million years old, far older than Homo sapiens , the modern human species. In 2023, the researchers - led by Jean-Michel Claverie of Aix-Marseille University in France - published a landmark study in the journal Viruses documenting the revival of ancient viruses from the Siberian permafrost. The report warned that accelerating permafrost thaw caused by climate change poses a potential public health threat by releasing dormant pathogens. Claverie’s team isolated 13 ancient viruses taken from locations across Siberia, belonging to five new viral groups. The oldest, a Pandoravirus yedoma , had been frozen solid beneath an underground lake for 48,500 years, while other, younger strains (around 27,000 years old) were extracted from the remains of a woolly mammoth’s stomach and from mammoth wool. Other researchers have noted that although the revived viruses were able to infect amoebas in lab conditions, it is unclear whether such viruses could infect animals or humans, or find a host outside a controlled laboratory. Claverie and his team cautioned at the time that unknowns remain buried in the permafrost, and a warming climate, which would also open previously untouched lands to deeper development, could expose people to pathogens that affect humans. In 2016, climate change played a role in unleashing anthrax in the remote Yamalo-Nenets region of Siberia, experts said at the time. Unusually high temperatures that summer, soaring to 95 degrees Fahrenheit, melted permafrost, and according to one hypothesis, exposed an infected reindeer carcass. The pathogen spread to living reindeer and eventually to a community of nomadic herders, where a 12-year-old boy died. item.title: Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters, letter shows
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Jacob Bogage and Andrew Goudsward WASHINGTON, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department on Tuesday gave California officials 48 hours to review a list of alleged noncitizen voters or face legal action, according to two letters reviewed by Reuters, part of an unprecedented effort to find evidence ‌of voter fraud ahead of next month's elections. The letters, written by acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter and addressed to California Secretary of State ‌Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan, say the Justice Department provided officials in Los Angeles County with a "password-protected thumb drive" with the names of people the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens" ​and were sent mail-in ballots from California. The letters demand that the state and county segregate returned mail-in ballots from voters on the Justice Department's list and not tabulate their votes "until citizenship has been determined." In cases where ballots have not been sent out yet, it orders California officials to withhold them from those on the list until their citizenship is confirmed. The federal government "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," according to the letters, if state and county officials do not follow its instructions. "Allowing noncitizens to vote cancels citizen votes," ‌McCotter wrote. The letters mark an escalation of the Trump administration's ⁠attempts to pressure states over alleged voting by non-US citizens and signal the Justice Department may be prepared to challenge ballots in the weeks leading up to the November 3 election, when Republicans will be defending their narrow majorities in Congress. Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten ⁠Pels confirmed the existence of the letters in a statement to Reuters, adding: "The department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law." Representatives from the White House and the California secretary of state's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Logan also did not immediately respond. FRAUD CLAIMS The Justice Department under President Donald Trump ​has ​repeatedly claimed that voting by non-US citizens is widespread, despite multiple studies showing it is rare. Though ​states may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to their voter ‌rolls since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, Reuters found in September, it was unclear how many had cast a ballot. Experts said the numbers were too small relative to the country's 170 million registered voters to affect elections. In July, the Justice Department sent letters to chief election officials in all 50 states warning they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allowed noncitizens to remain on their voter rolls or cast ballots. The department's Civil Rights Division has demanded nonpublic voter data, including voters' Social Security numbers or dates of birth, from nearly all states as part of its hunt for noncitizens on state rolls. It has sued 30 Democratic- and Republican-led states that ‌refused to hand over their rolls, but has lost 26 of those cases without winning one. Reuters reported ​last month that the Department of Homeland Security was using a commercial data broker to find sensitive ​voter information not included in publicly available rolls, which officials and experts ​warned could lead to citizens being falsely flagged as illegal voters and potentially detained. Federal prosecutors have also ramped up prosecutions of noncitizens ‌for allegedly voting in past elections or submitting fraudulent registrations, touting 16 ​new criminal cases on Monday. Officials in Democratic-led ​California have tussled for months with the Trump administration over its attempts to intervene in election procedures over allegations of voter fraud. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin informed California officials on July 16 that the federal government believed the state had noncitizens on its voting rolls, according to the letter. California could prove pivotal in ​deciding control of the US House of Representatives, especially after ‌the state's voters approved a new congressional map that heavily favors Democrats as part of a nationwide redistricting sprint that began in Republican-led states. Voters in ​Los Angeles will also weigh in on a ballot measure that would allow certain noncitizen legal residents to cast ballots in municipal elections. (Reporting by Jacob Bogage ​and Andrew Goudsward in Washington; Editing by Jesse Mesner-Hage, Jamie Freed and Daniel Wallis) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/exclusive-us-justice-department-threatens-034849746.html

item.title: Major U.S. banks turned away customers over political and religious views, report says
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Comptroller of the Currency says the nation's nine largest banks denied financial services to customers based on their political, religious, or social beliefs, according to a regulatory review released Wednesday. The OCC reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and received approximately 50,000 documents from JPMorgan Chase Bank, Bank of America, Citibank, Wells Fargo Bank, U.S. Bank, Capital One, PNC Bank, TD Bank, and BMO Bank regarding their policies, procedures, practices, and individual customer decisions. The federal banking watchdog determined that the banks' sweeping internal guidelines lacked objective, risk-based criteria, effectively shutting out legitimate customers and businesses based on ideological leanings rather than financial risk. The OCC said its findings reveal a systematic effort within the banking sector to restrict access for politically sensitive industries through both public and nonpublic policies. Federal regulators found that lenders restricted certain sectors' access to financial services, including oil and gas exploration; coal mining; firearms or ammunition manufacturing or distribution; construction or operation of detention facilities; and the manufacturing, distribution or online retail of tobacco or e-cigarettes. The Trump administration has voiced growing concerns over "de-banking" and the use of the financial system to achieve social and political objectives. "Today's report provides irrefutable evidence that the nation's largest banks have denied, debanked, and discriminated against customers and lawful businesses," said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould. "Americans should have access to financial services regardless of their beliefs, affiliations, or political views. " All nine banks report having reassessed the role of reputation risk in decisions to accept or terminate new customers, according to the OCC's report. Several banks said they had minimized reliance on reputation risk, and bank employees now must consider it in the context of other financial or business consequences, including credit risk, money laundering and terrorist financing risk. The Bank Policy Institute, a lobbying group that represents the banks, said in a statement in reaction to the report, "We support efforts to establish clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management, including the administration's recent efforts to prioritize supervisory attention on material financial risk and rather than reputational risk." The group also noted it would continue to work with the administration and Congress on proposals that ensure that political or religious beliefs do not unfairly affect customers' access to banking services. JPMorgan Chase said in a statement, "We take this seriously, learned from it, and improved the way we do business. We agree with the Administration on a broader point: years of operating in a regulatory environment that often second-guessed decisions contributed to a culture of caution across the banking industry. That system needs fixing." The bank says its policies prohibit discrimination against customers based on political or religious views. A spokesperson for Wells Fargo and Citigroup declined to comment on the OCC's report, while PNC said it was reviewing the findings. Bank of America, U.S. Bank and Capital One had not responded for comment as of this writing. The review was directed by President Trump's executive order, "Guaranteeing Fair Access to Banking for All Americans," to determine whether these banks' policies or practices required or influenced banks to deny or limit access to financial services to Americans because of their political or religious beliefs or lawful business activities. The OCC is considering further actions and writing new rules to prevent banks from discriminating against customers or prospective customers based on their political or religious beliefs. The OCC is also coordinating its debanking review with the reviews of other federal and state partners. "Notwithstanding certain efforts by the largest banks to rein in these practices, I am not confident that they will be enough," said Gould. item.title: Trump admin. delays IRS data that could show who benefited from GOP tax cuts
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The Trump administration is delaying the release of detailed data showing how Republicans’ 2025 tax cuts affected millions of Americans’ taxes, even as it tries to sell voters on the law ahead of the midterm elections. The numbers document which tax breaks were claimed by people in different income brackets, as well as information like how much they paid in taxes. The IRS typically releases the data in the wake of each filing season, and this year's rollout is more anticipated because it’s expected to provide the first detailed look at how taxpayers are taking advantage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including its new deductions for overtime wages and tipped income. The data was scheduled to be released in July, and then updated again in September, as the IRS processed more people’s returns —but the agency hasn't published either. The IRS said it is awaiting approval from the Treasury Department to publish the figures. But the delay has already irked some who complain it is part of a pattern of the administration withholding otherwise routine releases of tax data. “I think they are hiding stuff that doesn’t line up with all the crowing the CEO has been doing,” Nina Olson, a former national taxpayer advocate, said of Frank Bisignano, the IRS's day-to-day leader who has joined Republican lawmakers in touting the breaks to voters. The lack of detailed numbers on the 2026 filing season comes as the agency is also under fire for withholding a periodic report on the so-called tax gap, which is the share of taxes owed but not yet paid. The administration declined to answer questions about the delay on the record. In an emailed statement, an official speaking on condition of anonymity said its “priority is to release accurate and reliable data” following “major changes” to the tax code. The official did not say when the figures might be released. During the filing season, the IRS publishes weekly top-line statistics documenting how many returns it processed, how many refunds it issued and how much money taxpayers typically got back — figures the administration hyped earlier this year as evidence of the benefits of their tax cuts. But the delayed data is far more granular, showing the uptake of individual provisions in the code as well as things like how much more people in different income groups reported earning, and how many people still owed money to the IRS at the time of filing. In past years, the figures have created problems for the majority party when they didn’t show what lawmakers hoped for. Republicans took heat when the figures released the first year after their 2017 tax cuts showed fewer people taking deductions for charitable contributions, for example. It’s possible this year’s figures include less-than-flattering details about Republicans’ tax cuts — they could show the tax burden shifting between income groups, for instance, or a suspicious number of people claiming specific breaks, said Barry Johnson, a former top IRS official. But the reason why the data isn't out yet could also be more mundane, like if an unusual number of people requested filing extensions. “There’s all sorts of things it could be — you can’t know until you see the data whether it’s they don’t like the answers, or whether the data themselves really aren’t useful,” said Johnson, who was the IRS’s director of Statistics of Income from 2014 to 2025. But the Treasury isn’t supposed to be blocking the release of the figures, he said, pointing to a law Trump signed in his first term that gave statistical agencies, like at the IRS, more power to decide when to publish data. “By law, the IRS determines what they release and when it gets released,” said Johnson. “Treasury shouldn’t have a role in determining the timing of any statistical release. “It’s unusual,” he said. “It would telling to see if everything comes out in the middle of November, and then the stories a little bit challenging, then you’d say it was being held up to get past the midterms.” The first batch of data, showing figures through May, was originally slated for release in July, but is now listed on the IRS's website as “pending.” The update with numbers through July was slated to go out Sept. 17. The figures, when they're finally released, won’t be the final word on this filing season because they don’t include people who asked for filing extensions and now face an Oct. 15 deadline for completing their returns. Those taxpayers tend to be wealthier, so they tend to be understated in the figures. The mid-July data typically covers 95% of taxpayers, 87% of the income reported and 82% of the taxes paid, the IRS says. CORRECTION: A previous version of this story misstated Barry Johnson's title.This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/14/administration-delays-irs-data-gop-tax-cuts-01116807

item.title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey — and some of its cargo has survived
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say. They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built. The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside. The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. "The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Öniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition. The divers found three stone anchors, as ships carried spares on long voyages [Hakan Öniz] The wreck is close to the shore of Kekova Island in Antalya, Turkey. The artefacts lie scattered across an underwater slope, just 30m beneath the waves. Three large stone anchors were found, as well as more than 30 ceramic storage pots, called amphorae. The fact that none of the ship's wood remained meant techniques like radiocarbon dating - which measures a form of carbon in organic materials - could not be used to determine its age. Instead, archaeologists analysed the shape of the amphorae. Because pottery styles have changed over time, different styles are linked to particular periods. The Kekova ceramics are distinctive, with two handles, a ridge in the middle and a flat base. Öniz said this design matched other amphorae unearthed in Egypt and the Middle East that were known to be 4,400-4,700 years old. "Comparing the decoration techniques… we can definitely say our wreck is Early Bronze Age. This is 100%." The amphorae were recovered and taken on board the research ship [Hakan Öniz] After thousands of years underwater, the fragile artefacts are now being carefully conserved [Hakan Öniz] Divers from the expedition brought the pots up to the surface, where they are now being carefully conserved after so many thousands of years underwater. Dr Karin Sowada, an archaeologist from Macquarie University, Australia, examined the amphorae after they were recovered. Some were intact and she was surprised to see they still contained a viscous, glossy residue. "I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots…. a lot of this material was still remaining," she said. The team is now working to find out exactly what was being carried in the amphorae. "It could be olive oil, it could be wine, it could be tree resins," Sowada said. "It's possible that [the residue] could actually be the result of reuse of the jars. I mean, these jars are huge - they're not things that you just ship away and then never see again. People would have emptied these jars on arrival and potentially used them for many, many, many years." [BBC] The wreck and its cargo are also shedding light on trade in the ancient world. The archaeologists say the ship started its voyage from somewhere along the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. They believe it was taking goods to either the ancient city of Troy, in what is now north-western Turkey, or to the Minoan people in Crete. The divers worked underwater to carefully excavate the artefacts [Hakan Öniz] Travelling by sea was fraught with danger, particularly around Kekova Island, where the strong currents and winds have claimed many ships. There are hundreds of wrecks in the area, and the Mediterranean Archaeology Association specialises in finding and studying them. Öniz says that when he is diving on the wreck his first thoughts are about the lives of the people who were connected to this vessel. "We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years. "We are always thinking of the sailors... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back." The shipwreck is owned by the Turkish Ministry of Culture. Its minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said the artefacts that have been recovered would be put on display in the new Mediterranean Underwater Archaeology Museum in Antalya when it opens in the coming months. The depth meant the divers could only spend 30 minutes at a time exploring it [Hakan Öniz] The Kekova discovery now tops the list of the world's oldest shipwrecks. Previously, the record holder was a wreck off the coast of Dokos, an island in southern Greece, which dates to about 4,200 years ago. The oldest known intact shipwreck, where the wood is still preserved, was found in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria. It dates to about 2,400 years ago. item.title: House control all but gone, top Republicans privately concede
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Some top congressional Republicans have privately concluded that it is likely impossible for them to keep control of the House of Representatives in the midterm elections, and they are now focused on limiting the scale of the defeat and salvaging the party’s Senate majority. Five senior Republican lawmakers, all granted anonymity to speak candidly about their party’s dire position, told POLITICO the House had all but slipped away. One senior House Republican said the GOP’s goal at this point was to “save as many Republican seats as we can.” The president, this person said, was not helping. “President Trump has made this election all about himself,” the lawmaker said. “Now we have to survive that political storm.” A second Republican member of Congress said the movement of campaign advertising made plain which side was in control of the midterms. This lawmaker predicted Democrats would pick up about 10 seats, more than enough to take control of the chamber. Even in newly redistricted red states like Florida and Texas, this person said, Republican candidates were “hanging on with their fingernails.” Republicans have already fallen back from several contested House districts that they feel are no longer winnable, including those held by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa and Tom Kean Jr. of New Jersey. Trump carried their districts just two years ago. The party last week gave up on an Omaha-based district held by retiring Rep. Don Bacon. Trump officials and other top GOP operatives say more candidates may be cut off in the coming days, in order to shift advertising money to races where it can make more of a difference. Republican groups have already given up on multiple races where they once hoped to unseat Democratic lawmakers. The Republican Party is under extreme pressure across the Midwest, where it is now spending heavily to defend Senate seats in once-reliably MAGA states like Iowa, Nebraska and Kansas. Bacon, a maverick often at odds with the White House, said there was no mystery in his party’s political tribulations. “I’ve talked to some who are making these decisions: The biggest problem is the president’s polling numbers and unfavorables,” Bacon said. White House officials insist they’re not giving up on either chamber of Congress. In a statement, White House spokeswoman Liz Huston said Trump remained “committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate.” As he departed Tuesday to campaign in Alaska for embattled GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, Trump professed optimism about the midterms but acknowledged that sitting presidents typically see their party lose seats in the off year. “But I'm doing a tour right now and I'm doing rallies,” Trump added. “The level of enthusiasm for the Republican Party is way up.” House Speaker Mike Johnson went even further, flatly declaring during a campaign stop in deep-red Texas that “the polling is wrong” in showing his party on the brink of a broad defeat. Yet at a tactical level, the Republican Party’s shift in focus away from defending the House and toward saving the Senate is clear enough. In recent days, the Congressional Leadership Fund, the top super PAC for House Republicans, canceled advertising for key House candidates in Nebraska and Iowa to move that money to other House races. That allowed the Senate Leadership Fund — a Republican group focused on the upper chamber — to swoop in and claim the airtime to support Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts and Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Senate in Iowa. “These are not the moves of a party that’s going to keep the House,” a third Republican lawmaker said. In statements to POLITICO, both CLF and the National Republican Congressional Committee said they had no intention of giving up on the fight for control of the House. NRCC spokesperson Mike Marinella said districts are won "one by one," and that the GOP has "the financial firepower and ground game needed to win." Chris Winkelman, president of CLF, said his group would keep moving money around to maximize the impact nationally. The goal, he said, was to “keep the pressure on the most vulnerable Democrats and preserve a path to 218 seats.” Former Rep. Carlos Curbelo, a Florida Republican who lost his swing seat in Trump’s first midterm election eight years ago, said his former colleagues were clear-eyed about where the election seemed to be headed. “The environment is about as tough as one could expect,” Curbelo said. “There is no one who has privately stated that they believe Republicans can hold the House — not in recent weeks, anyway.” Megan Messerly, Lauren Fedor, Lisa Kashinsky and Myah Ward contributed to this report.
